item.title: UAT-7810 LONGLEASH ORB, ScoutC2 Detection, and npm/PyPI Payment Typosquats
item.content:encoded:
Chinese hackers develop LONGLEASH malware to expand ORB network — Must Read

Chinese threat actor UAT-7810 is expanding an ORB proxy network by exploiting unpatched internet-facing routers, especially Ruckus devices, and deploying upgraded LONGLEASH malware. The infrastructure helps China-aligned APTs hide traffic through compromised local devices and evade detection.

  • Cisco Talos researchers report that Chinese hackers tracked as UAT-7810 are expanding an Operational Relay Box network by compromising internet-facing networking devices, primarily unpatched Ruckus routers.
  • The ORB network serves as secure relay infrastructure for other China-aligned advanced persistent threats, including UAT-5918, by proxying traffic through regional devices to evade detection and complicate attribution.
  • Talos identified new malware and tools in the campaign, including LONGLEASH, DOGLEASH, JARLEASH, and LEASHTEST.
  • UAT-7810 primarily exploits known vulnerabilities for initial access, including CVE-2020-22653, CVE-2020-22658, and CVE-2023-25717 in Ruckus routers, as well as CVE-2025-2492 in ASUS AiCloud routers.
  • LONGLEASH is an upgraded version of SHORTLEASH with added capabilities including reverse shell access, multiple proxying methods, SMTP client and server functionality, TLS and PKI support, self-removal, and intermediate command-and-control forwarding.

Coordinated npm and PyPI Campaign Typosquats Popular Secure Payment Apps — Should Read

Socket found a coordinated npm and PyPI typosquatting campaign impersonating PaySafe, Skrill, and Neteller SDKs to steal API keys, tokens, and other environment secrets from developers and CI systems. Affected users should remove the packages, block the ngrok C2 domain, and rotate any exposed secrets immediately.

  • Socket’s AI scanner detected 17 malicious npm and PyPI packages published nearly simultaneously on July 7, 2026, targeting SDK developers and users of PaySafe, Skrill, and Neteller payment applications.
  • The npm packages published four malicious versions each, while the PyPI packages published one malicious version each at the time of publication.
  • The packages mimic payment SDK clients but steal credentials and tokens from environment variables and exfiltrate the data to the hostname caliber-spinner-finishing.ngrok-free.dev.
  • The malware includes sandbox evasion checks, skipping exfiltration when fewer than two CPU cores are present or when hostnames or usernames contain terms such as sandbox, analyzer, cuckoo, virus, malware, vmware, or vbox.
  • The article recommends rotating all secrets on any machine that imported or executed the packages, searching dependency trees for the listed package names, blocking them at the registry proxy level, and hunting outbound HTTPS traffic to .ngrok-free.dev from build or CI hosts.

OMB M-26-14: Why federal agencies must fix asset visibility first — Should Read

OMB M-26-14 makes complete asset visibility the foundation for federal logging maturity, requiring agencies to prove increasing IT, OT, and IoT inventory coverage before they can meet log collection milestones. Agencies should close asset discovery gaps before CISA’s logging reference architecture starts the compliance clock.

  • OMB M-26-14 rescinds M-21-31 and replaces blanket data-retention mandates with a risk-based logging maturity model based on five elements: inventory visibility, collection coverage, collection operations, data retention, and log management.
  • The maturity model requires agencies to capture 70%, 80%, 90%, and 95% of IT, OT, and IoT assets in centralized inventories at levels 1 through 4, respectively.
  • Overall maturity is calculated using the lowest-performing element, so an agency with strong log collection but weak inventory visibility receives the lower overall maturity level.
  • The directive explicitly includes IoT devices and operational technology systems, including systems owned, operated, or managed by third parties.
  • Once CISA publishes the logging reference architecture, agencies must submit an Agency Logging Plan within 90 days and reach levels 1, 2, and 3 within 120, 180, and 320 days, respectively.

Detecting ScoutC2 Malware Through HTTP Artifacts | Corelight — May Read

Corelight explains how ScoutC2 command-and-control activity can be detected through distinctive HTTP artifacts in network traffic. The key takeaway is that defenders can use HTTP telemetry to spot ScoutC2 infections even when endpoint evidence is limited.

  • The article focuses on ScoutC2 malware.
  • The article discusses detecting ScoutC2 malware through HTTP artifacts.
  • The article is presented by Corelight.

Top Burp Suite alternatives for web application security testing — Optional

The article argues that Burp Suite remains strong for manual web app testing, but teams needing CI/CD-native DAST, broader AppSec coverage, API discovery, and autonomous AI pentesting may be better served by newer alternatives. It positions Aikido Security as the top option for those needs, with Caido, ZAP, and Invicti/Acunetix fitting more specific use cases.

  • Burp Suite is a web application security testing tool from PortSwigger built around an intercepting proxy that lets testers inspect and modify traffic between a browser and a target application.
  • PortSwigger offers Burp Suite Community, Burp Suite Professional, and Burp Suite DAST, with Community lacking automated scanning, Professional adding Burp Scanner and Burp AI, and DAST supporting CI/CD integrations and portfolio-scale scanning.
  • The article says teams look for Burp Suite alternatives because they want CI/CD-native DAST, autonomous AI pentesting, API discovery beyond configured specs and crawls, broader code-to-cloud coverage, and automated remediation.
  • The article ranks Aikido Security as the strongest Burp Suite alternative for teams that want DAST and continuous AI pentesting, citing authenticated testing, live-traffic API discovery, attack surface management, code-to-cloud coverage, and AutoFix pull requests.
  • The article identifies Caido as a lightweight modern proxy for individual testers, ZAP as a free open-source DAST option, and Invicti or Acunetix as proof-based scanning tools for enterprise or mid-market AppSec teams.
